C009.note: This does not make Vasiṣṭha the identified speaker, nor establish a historical sibling relationship.

C010.subject: vedic
C010.summary: The verse explicitly says Agastya roused the Aśvins with praises.

C011.subject: vedic
C011.summary: The hymn recalls aid given to Atri.
C011.note: Hymn attribution is not a statement that Agastya personally met Atri.

C012.subject: vedic
C012.summary: Tugra’s son is invoked as a precedent.
C012.note: Retain the wording Tugra’s son; do not automatically resolve to a unique Bhujyu.

C015.subject: rama
C015.summary: Rāma recounts Agastya’s deeds en route to his hermitage.
C015.speaker: Rāma

C016.subject: sutikshna
C016.summary: Sutīkṣṇa directs the party toward Agastya.
C016.speaker: Sutīkṣṇa

C017.subject: lakshmana
C017.summary: Lakṣmaṇa asks Agastya’s disciple to announce their arrival.
C017.speaker: Lakṣmaṇa
C017.note: The request is made to a disciple; it is not direct speech to Agastya.

C018.subject: rama
C018.summary: Rāma asks the sage where to reside.
C018.speaker: Rāma

C019.subject: ramayana
C019.summary: Agastya advises Rāma about residence and Sītā.
C019.speaker: Agastya

C021.subject: ramayana
C021.summary: Agastya praises Sītā’s endurance and fidelity.
C021.speaker: Agastya

C022.subject: ramayana
C022.summary: Agastya states his friendship with Daśaratha.
C022.speaker: Agastya

C023.subject: ramayana
C023.summary: Arundhatī is the comparison for Sītā.
C023.speaker: Agastya

C026.subject: sugriva
C026.summary: Sugrīva directs the southern search party toward Agastya.
C026.speaker: Sugrīva

C028.subject: ramayana
C028.summary: Agastya instructs Rāma to worship the sun.
C028.speaker: Agastya

C030.subject: yudhisthira
C030.summary: Yudhiṣṭhira asks why Agastya killed Vātāpi.
C030.speaker: Yudhiṣṭhira
C030.note: He asks Lomaśa, not Agastya; no meeting is asserted.

C032.subject: mahabharata
C032.summary: Agastya asks the Vidarbha ruler for Lopāmudrā.
C032.speaker: Agastya

C033.subject: mahabharata
C033.summary: The spouses discuss household life and wealth.
C033.speaker: Agastya

C036.subject: mahabharata
C036.summary: Agastya requests wealth without harm to others.
C036.speaker: Agastya

C037.subject: mahabharata
C037.summary: Agastya requests wealth without harm to others.
C037.speaker: Agastya

C038.subject: mahabharata
C038.summary: Agastya requests wealth without harm to others.
C038.speaker: Agastya
C038.note: Trasadasyu is called Purukutsa’s son here; cross-text identity with a Vedic king remains untested.

C039.subject: mahabharata
C039.summary: Agastya addresses Ilvala about Vātāpi and wealth.
C039.speaker: Agastya

C041.subject: mahabharata
C041.summary: The son is called Dṛḍhasyu and also Idhmavāha.
C041.note: Keep this epic identity local to its witness; later Vedic attribution indexes may differ.

C045.subject: salya
C045.summary: Śalya narrates Agastya’s report to Indra.
C045.speaker: Śalya

C046.subject: indra
C046.summary: Indra asks Agastya how Nahuṣa fell.
C046.speaker: Indra

C047.subject: mahabharata
C047.summary: Agastya tells Indra about Nahuṣa’s fall.
C047.speaker: Agastya

C048.subject: mahabharata
C048.summary: Agastya recounts cursing Nahuṣa to serpent existence.
C048.speaker: Agastya
C048.note: Ganguli gives ten thousand years for the curse; this is not Agastya’s age.

C051.subject: puranic
C051.summary: The verse assigns shared Mitra–Varuṇa parentage.
C051.note: Mythic genealogy, not independently dated biological evidence.

C052.subject: puranic
C052.summary: The verse assigns shared Mitra–Varuṇa parentage.
C052.note: Mythic genealogy, not independently dated biological evidence.

C053.subject: puranic
C053.summary: The two sages share the stated parentage.

C054.subject: puranic
C054.summary: Urvaśī appears in the jar-birth context.
C054.note: Do not flatten this into an ordinary mother–son relationship.

C055.subject: puranic
C055.summary: Agastya curses the silent king to elephant existence.
C055.speaker: Agastya

C059.subject: naccinarkkiniyar
C059.summary: The commentator links Tolkāppiyar to Agastya.
C059.source_title: Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature

C060.subject: peraciriyar
C060.source_title: Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature

C061.subject: tamil
C061.summary: Tolkāppiyar is presented as Agastya’s pupil.
C061.note: A commentary tradition; not an explicit statement in the Tolkāppiyam base text.
C061.source_title: Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature

C065.subject: tamil
C065.summary: The Vēḷir accompany the southern migration.

C067.subject: tamil
C067.summary: The Buddhist tradition makes Avalokiteśvara the teacher.

C068.subject: tamil
C068.summary: Another tradition assigns the instruction to Śiva.

VEX001.subject: vedic
VEX001.summary: The hymn voice asks the Maruts to set aside their anger and forgive the speaker after Soma intended for them was given away.
VEX001.speaker: Agastya according to hymn attribution and editorial speaker division
VEX001.note: Speaker divisions are an editorial reconstruction; the hymn itself does not identify each speech by speaker name.
VEX001.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX002.subject: vedic
VEX002.summary: The speaker asks Indra and the Maruts to be reconciled and prosper together.
VEX002.speaker: Agastya according to hymn attribution and editorial speaker division
VEX002.note: The object Indra is paired with the Maruts in the passage; predicate describes the requested action.
VEX002.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX003.subject: indra
VEX003.summary: Agastya says to Indra that the Maruts are Indra’s brothers.
VEX003.speaker: Agastya in the editorial speaker division
VEX003.note: This wording is in 1.170.2, not 1.171.2; attribution of the speech is based on editorial verse divisions.
VEX003.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX004.subject: vedic
VEX004.summary: The verse asks Indra together with the Maruts to grant fame and strength to the sons of Māna; the commentary identifies Māna as Agastya’s father.
VEX004.speaker: Agastya by hymn attribution
VEX004.note: “Sons of Māna” is in 1.171.5. The identification of Māna as Agastya’s father is commentary. Do not merge him automatically with a Māna in RV 7.33.
VEX004.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX005.subject: vedic
VEX005.summary: Jamison and Brereton read 1.165, 1.170, and 1.171 together as a poetic sequence about Agastya’s offering and a dispute between Indra and the Maruts.
VEX005.note: This is a modern reconstruction of a story across hymns, not an explicit continuous narrative in one passage.
VEX005.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX006.subject: vedic
VEX006.locator: Ṛgveda 1.165, speaker divisions and introduction, pp. 360–361
VEX006.summary: In the editorial division of 1.165, the closing verses assigned to Agastya address the Maruts and offer them his hymn.
VEX006.speaker: Agastya according to hymn attribution and editorial speaker division
VEX006.note: Jamison–Brereton assign 1.165.13–15 to Agastya; the dialogue structure and individual speakers are editorially analyzed.
VEX006.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX007.subject: vedic
VEX007.summary: The three-verse Marut hymn 1.172 is identified in the edition as a short pendant to Agastya’s Indra–Marut hymn cycle.
VEX007.note: Traditional/editorial hymn attribution does not establish personal authorship or a historical encounter.
VEX007.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX008.subject: mitra
VEX008.summary: The translation calls the lightning-radiance seen by Mitra and Varuṇa one of Vasiṣṭha’s births, and mentions another when Agastya brings him to the clan.
VEX008.note: Jamison–Brereton render this as one of two births; Griffith renders “one and only birth.” This claim follows the former without asserting historical biography.
VEX008.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX009.subject: varuna
VEX009.summary: The translation calls the lightning-radiance seen by Mitra and Varuṇa one of Vasiṣṭha’s births, and mentions another when Agastya brings him to the clan.
VEX009.note: Jamison–Brereton render this as one of two births; Griffith renders “one and only birth.” This claim follows the former without asserting historical biography.
VEX009.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX010.subject: vasistha
VEX010.summary: Griffith translates Vasiṣṭha as the son of Varuṇa and Mitra.
VEX010.note: The verse belongs to a layered mythic account and does not establish historical parentage.

VEX011.subject: vasistha
VEX011.summary: The verse describes Vasiṣṭha as born from Urvaśī, from her mind.
VEX011.note: Griffith instead renders the passage “Born of their love for Urvasi”; the wording here follows Jamison–Brereton.
VEX011.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX012.subject: vasistha
VEX012.summary: The verse calls Agastya bringing Vasiṣṭha here for the clan another of Vasiṣṭha’s births.
VEX012.note: Jamison–Brereton render viśa as “clan”; Griffith says Agastya brought him hither from his stock.
VEX012.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

VEX013.subject: mitra
VEX013.summary: The hymn says the two gods poured their seed together into a vessel during a ritual gathering.
VEX013.note: The verse then names Māna as arising from the middle and says that the sage Vasiṣṭha was born from him; do not equate Māna with Agastya.

VEX014.subject: vedic
VEX014.summary: The verse associates the Aśvins’ restoration of Viśpalā with praise and poetic formulation by Agastya.
VEX014.note: The verse mentions Agastya in the third person; it does not say that he met Viśpalā or personally witnessed the event.
VEX014.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

EEX001.subject: rama
EEX001.summary: Agastya gives Rama a divine bow, inexhaustible quivers and a sword, describing them as weapons once used by Viṣṇu.
EEX001.speaker: Agastya
EEX001.note: A narrated gift at their meeting; introductory commentary on the page is excluded.

EEX002.subject: lakshmana
EEX002.summary: Lakṣmaṇa introduces himself to Agastya’s disciple as Rama’s younger brother and says the brothers entered the forest at their father’s order.
EEX002.speaker: Lakṣmaṇa
EEX002.note: Reported speech to the disciple, before the meeting with Agastya.

EEX003.subject: rama
EEX003.summary: Lakṣmaṇa identifies Rama as Daśaratha’s eldest son when requesting an audience with Agastya.
EEX003.speaker: Lakṣmaṇa
EEX003.note: The relationship is stated in an audience request, not as a separate chronology date.

EEX004.subject: sita
EEX004.summary: Lakṣmaṇa identifies Sītā as Rama’s wife while announcing their arrival at Agastya’s hermitage.
EEX004.speaker: Lakṣmaṇa
EEX004.note: Directly stated in reported speech to the disciple.

EEX005.subject: sutikshna
EEX005.summary: After spending time with Sutīkṣṇa, Rama takes leave and proceeds to visit Agastya; the account places this visit after the narrated ten-year period among nearby hermitages.
EEX005.note: The ten years belong to Rama’s itinerary in this narrative, not to Agastya’s age.

EEX007.subject: epic_pitrs
EEX007.summary: Agastya’s suspended ancestors tell him that they remain in that state for want of his offspring and ask him to beget a son.
EEX007.speaker: Agastya’s ancestors, in Lomasa’s narration
EEX007.note: The episode motivates the marriage and progeny narrative; it is a narrated past, not a meeting with Yudhiṣṭhira.

EEX008.subject: vidarbha_king
EEX008.summary: The unnamed Vidarbha king is unwilling to give his daughter but fears Agastya’s curse if he refuses.
EEX008.speaker: Lomasa
EEX008.note: The king remains unnamed in this passage; not assigned another identity.

EEX009.subject: lopamudra
EEX009.summary: Seeing her parents distressed, Lopāmudrā tells her father to give her to Agastya and spare himself anxiety.
EEX009.speaker: Lomasa
EEX009.note: The daughter’s own consent is explicit in this telling.

EEX010.subject: lopamudra
EEX010.summary: After their marriage, Agastya and Lopāmudrā go to Gaṅgādvāra and practice austerities together.
EEX010.speaker: Lomasa
EEX010.note: Narrated after the marriage; this is a narrative sequence, with no absolute date.

EEX011.subject: lopamudra
EEX011.summary: Before agreeing to marital intercourse, Lopāmudrā asks Agastya for a bed, adornments and attire like those she had in her father’s palace.
EEX011.speaker: Lomasa
EEX011.note: This request motivates Agastya’s subsequent search for wealth; no modern chronological inference is implied.

EEX012.subject: srutarvan
EEX012.summary: After declining to take wealth from Śrutarvan because his income matched his expenses, Agastya takes that king with him to Vṛdhnaśva.
EEX012.speaker: Lomasa
EEX012.note: Narrative sequence among named kings; Ganguli section locator is not a BORI chapter number.

EEX013.subject: vradhnasva
EEX013.summary: Vṛdhnaśva offers wealth, but Agastya declines because the king’s income equals his expenditure; Vṛdhnaśva then joins Agastya and Śrutarvan in visiting Trasadasyu.
EEX013.speaker: Lomasa
EEX013.note: The passage calls Trasadasyu Purokutsa’s son and places him in Ikṣvāku’s line; this epic witness is not identified with Vedic namesakes.

EEX014.subject: ilvala
EEX014.summary: Lomasa says Ilvala transforms his brother Vātāpi into a ram, serves his cooked flesh to Brahmins, then summons him to emerge and kill them.
EEX014.speaker: Lomasa
EEX014.note: Narrated background for the later encounter; it is not a separate meeting between Agastya and the brothers.

EEX015.subject: mahabharata
EEX015.summary: At Ilvala’s feast Agastya eats the served Vātāpi and says he has digested him before he can emerge.
EEX015.speaker: Lomasa
EEX015.note: The narrative presents the act as defeating the brothers’ recurring killing stratagem.

EEX016.subject: ilvala
EEX016.summary: Ilvala gives Agastya the wealth the sage names, including twice the amount offered to each king, a golden chariot and two horses.
EEX016.speaker: Lomasa
EEX016.note: Agastya states the intended gift; Ilvala checks and then gives it. The named kings also receive wealth.

EEX017.subject: dridhasyu
EEX017.summary: Lomasa says the foetus remained in Lopāmudrā’s womb seven years before Dṛḍhasyu was born; as a child he carried sacrificial fuel and was called Idhmavāha.
EEX017.speaker: Lomasa
EEX017.note: The epithet and the seven-year gestation belong to this epic story; they do not independently date Agastya or identify a different Dṛḍhasyu.

EEX018.subject: epic_pitrs
EEX018.summary: The narration says Agastya’s ancestors obtain the desired state after he begets Dṛḍhasyu.
EEX018.speaker: Lomasa
EEX018.note: This is the story’s stated consequence of the son’s birth.

EEX020.subject: nahusha
EEX020.summary: In Agastya’s account to Indra, Nahuṣa touches the sage’s head with his foot while the sages carry him; Agastya then curses him to fall from heaven and roam as a serpent for ten thousand years.
EEX020.speaker: Agastya, in Śalya’s narration
EEX020.note: This adds the trigger and sequence to the core curse claim. Ten thousand years describes Nahuṣa’s curse, not Agastya’s lifespan.

TEX_002.subject: tolkappiyar
TEX_002.summary: Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s commentary on the Tolkāppiyam preface identifies Tolkāppiyar as Tiraṇatūmākkiṉi, son of Camata(k)kiṉi, and a pupil of Akattiyar.
TEX_002.speaker: Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar as reported by Zvelebil
TEX_002.note: The attribution belongs to the commentator’s account, not to an explicit statement in the Tolkāppiyam base text.
TEX_002.source_title: Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature

TEX_003.subject: peraciriyar
TEX_003.summary: Pērāciriyar acknowledges a view that Tolkāppiyar followed other now-lost grammatical works, then argues that he was Akattiyar’s foremost pupil and followed his teaching.
TEX_003.speaker: Pērāciriyar as reported by Zvelebil
TEX_003.note: Reports a debate among commentators and scholars; it does not establish a historical teacher-pupil relationship.
TEX_003.source_title: Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature

TEX_004.subject: peraciriyar
TEX_004.summary: Zvelebil reports Pērāciriyar’s attribution to Akattiyan of Tamil’s three divisions: iyal, icai, and nāṭakam; he also describes Akattiyam as the foundational text for Tolkāppiyam.
TEX_004.speaker: Pērāciriyar as reported by Zvelebil
TEX_004.note: These are statements attributed to the commentary, not surviving contents of a complete Akattiyam.
TEX_004.source_title: Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature

TEX_005.subject: tamil
TEX_005.summary: In canto 1, the sage Agastya tells the named Chola king Chembiyan Cheralāthan to hold an Indra festival at Pukār; the king agrees and invites Indra for twenty-eight days.
TEX_005.speaker: Narrator
TEX_005.note: A named Agastya appearance in the translated base poem; the narrated setting supplies no historical date for the sage.
TEX_005.source_title: Maṇimēkalai · English translation by Kausalya Hart

TEX_007.subject: tamil_kanthan
TEX_007.summary: King Kānthan says he will seek the sage Agastya’s grace to resolve his troubles.
TEX_007.speaker: King Kānthan in quoted speech
TEX_007.note: The episode names Agastya inside the narrative; it does not date the episode historically.
TEX_007.source_title: Maṇimēkalai · English translation by Kausalya Hart

TEX_008.subject: velir
TEX_008.summary: Kapilar’s poem praises a Vēḷ chief as descended through forty-nine generations from a lineage said to arise from an unnamed northern sage’s vessel and rule Tuvarai.
TEX_008.speaker: Kapilar in the poem, as translated by Mahadevan
TEX_008.note: Mahadevan paraphrases Puṟanāṉūṟu 201 and separately proposes identifying the unnamed sage as Agastya. The poem itself and its translation have not been independently checked here.
TEX_008.source_title: Puṟanāṉūṟu 201 · literal translation excerpt in Mahadevan

TEX_009.subject: naccinarkkiniyar
TEX_009.summary: Mahadevan reports that Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s Tolkāppiyam commentary has Akattiyar lead eighteen Vēḷir families, eighteen kings, and Aruvaḷar from Tuvarāpati south, with Potiyil as his eventual abode.
TEX_009.speaker: Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar as reported by Mahadevan
TEX_009.note: This is a commentary narrative reported by a modern scholar. Tuvarāpati = Dvārakā is an identification, and the story supplies no verified migration date.

REX002.subject: root_udayin
REX002.summary: Udāyin names Agastya while arguing with the prince.
REX002.speaker: Udāyin
REX002.note: A character’s retrospective example; not a meeting with Agastya.
REX002.source_title: Buddhacarita, Book IV, The Women Rejected

REX003.subject: root_udayin
REX003.summary: The prince hears and answers Udāyin’s arguments.
REX003.speaker: Udāyin and the prince
REX003.note: This links the referring voice to its narrative audience, not the prince to Agastya personally.
REX003.source_title: Buddhacarita, Book IV, The Women Rejected

REX004.subject: buddhist
REX004.summary: Udāyin’s example says Agastya desired Rohiṇī.
REX004.speaker: Udāyin
REX004.note: Narrative allegation in a rhetorical example, not independent biographical confirmation.

REX005.subject: root_rohini
REX005.summary: The verse identifies Rohiṇī as Soma’s wife.
REX005.speaker: Udāyin

REX006.subject: buddhist
REX006.summary: The same verse also names Lopāmudrā.
REX006.speaker: Udāyin
REX006.note: Cowell’s English for the second half of 4.73 is difficult; this records co-mention only, without inferring kinship or a second event.

REX008.subject: lopamudra
REX008.summary: Lopāmudrā is assigned the first two verses.
REX008.speaker: Lopāmudrā, by Bṛhaddevatā attribution

REX009.subject: vedic
REX009.summary: Agastya is assigned the next two verses.
REX009.speaker: Agastya, by Bṛhaddevatā attribution

REX010.subject: root_student
REX010.summary: The unnamed student is assigned the concluding verses.
REX010.note: This student belongs to an explanatory tradition; no personal name is supplied.

REX011.subject: vedic
REX011.summary: The sage and his wife reassure their student.
REX011.speaker: Agastya and Lopāmudrā
REX011.note: Later reception of the hymn, not an extra verse of the Ṛgveda; unproofread OCR.

REX012.subject: vedic
REX012.summary: The catalogue assigns this praise to Agastya.
REX012.note: A later hymn catalogue’s attribution; original hymns require their own source-level reading. Unproofread OCR.

REX013.subject: vedic
REX013.summary: The catalogue assigns this praise to Agastya.
REX013.note: A later hymn catalogue’s attribution; original hymns require their own source-level reading. Unproofread OCR.

REX014.subject: vedic
REX014.summary: The catalogue assigns this praise to Agastya.
REX014.note: A later hymn catalogue’s attribution; original hymns require their own source-level reading. Unproofread OCR.

REX015.subject: vedic
REX015.summary: The catalogue assigns this praise to Agastya.
REX015.note: A later hymn catalogue’s attribution; original hymns require their own source-level reading. Unproofread OCR.

REX016.subject: vedic
REX016.summary: The catalogue assigns this praise to Agastya.
REX016.note: A later hymn catalogue’s attribution; original hymns require their own source-level reading. Unproofread OCR.

V3H001.subject: vedic_vasisthas
V3H001.summary: The hymn credits the Vasiṣṭhas’ sacred formulation with bringing Indra’s help to Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings.
V3H001.speaker: Ṛgveda 7.33 hymn voice; speaker division follows Jamison–Brereton’s editorial reading
V3H001.note: This is a claim within the hymn’s account, not independent historical confirmation. The collective Vasiṣṭhas is retained; it is not collapsed into one individual poet.
V3H001.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

V3H002.subject: vedic_vasisthas
V3H002.summary: The verse says Indra, acting with the Vasiṣṭhas, smashed Bheda.
V3H002.speaker: Ṛgveda 7.33 hymn voice; plural referent follows the translation’s ‘with them’
V3H002.note: The action is attributed to Indra; the Vasiṣṭhas are companions/ritual supporters in the verse. This records the hymn’s presentation, not a verified battle report.
V3H002.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

V3H003.subject: vasistha
V3H003.locator: Ṛgveda 7.33.1–14; edition heading and translation, pp. 923–924
V3H003.summary: The hymn moves from Vasiṣṭha and his descendants (verses 1–9) to Vasiṣṭha’s birth narrative (verses 10–14).
V3H003.speaker: Jamison–Brereton’s edition heading and segmentation
V3H003.note: This is a same-hymn narrative link, not a claim of biological kinship. The verse segmentation and collective-versus-individual distinction are editorial framing.
V3H003.source_title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India

E3H001.subject: rama
E3H001.summary: While proceeding toward Pañcavaṭī, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa encounter Jaṭāyu; Jaṭāyu identifies himself as a friend of Daśaratha, and Rāma accepts and honors him.
E3H001.speaker: Narrator; Jaṭāyu identifies himself in reported speech
E3H001.note: This is Rāma's meeting with Jaṭāyu after Agastya's direction to Pañcavaṭī; the passage does not depict Jaṭāyu meeting Agastya.

E3H002.subject: jatayu
E3H002.summary: Jaṭāyu says that he was born from Aruṇa.
E3H002.speaker: Jaṭāyu, speaking to Rāma
E3H002.note: A source-local Rāmāyaṇa genealogy claim; this witness should not be merged automatically with other Aruṇa traditions.

E3H003.subject: jatayu
E3H003.summary: Jaṭāyu identifies Sampāti as his elder brother.
E3H003.speaker: Jaṭāyu, speaking to Rāma
E3H003.note: The passage also says they belong to Aruṇa's lineage.

E3H004.subject: jatayu
E3H004.summary: Jaṭāyu identifies himself as Śyenī's son.
E3H004.speaker: Jaṭāyu, speaking to Rāma
E3H004.note: The passage gives both this parentage and birth from Aruṇa; both statements are retained without reconciling their genealogy.

TPH001.subject: tamil_kanthan
TPH001.summary: In the sages’ story, King Kānthan chooses Kahandan, described as a courtesan’s son, to rule while he leaves the city.
TPH001.speaker: Sages narrating to the king
TPH001.note: This supplies a passage-supported second edge from the Agastya-related Kānthan episode. It is not evidence of a meeting between Agastya and Kahandan.
